title: FDA Names Romaine and Parsley in Two Outbreaks — 12 Weeks Late, and No Farm or Brand Named
excerpt: The FDA closed two foodborne illness investigations on Nov. 4, finally naming romaine lettuce and parsley as the likely sources of outbreaks that sickened…
content:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration closed two foodborne illness investigations on Nov. 4, finally naming romaine lettuce and parsley as the likely sources of outbreaks that sickened 218 people combined — but only after the food was past its shelf life, and without naming any grower, brand, processor, distributor or state, according to the FDA and Food Safety News.

The Salmonella outbreak, tracked as ref #1402, sickened 43 people, with romaine lettuce identified as the likely source, according to the FDA. The outbreak was first posted to the FDA's CORE outbreak table on Aug. 12, 2026, with the product listed as "Not Yet Identified" — about 12 weeks before romaine was named, according to the Marler Blog.

The Cyclospora outbreak, ref #1392, was also closed Nov. 4, with parsley identified as the likely source and its case count cut from 241 to 175, according to the FDA. The 66 cases removed were moved into a new Cyclospora outbreak, ref #1396, because of "differences identified during the traceback investigation" — and its food remains unidentified.

In both investigations, all FDA environmental samples tested negative — for Salmonella in the romaine investigation and for Cyclospora in the parsley investigation, according to the FDA.

Why the public learned so little, so late

The FDA said that by the time investigators confirmed each food as the source, the products were past shelf life and no longer for sale, and that "this outbreak has ended, and there is no risk to consumers," according to the FDA. That assurance applies only to those specific expired products — not to romaine or parsley in general.

The FDA released no patient ages, locations, hospitalization counts or illness onset dates for either outbreak, according to Food Safety News and the Marler Blog. No Texas case count was published for either outbreak.

The same day, the FDA also closed a 119-case Salmonella Newport outbreak, ref #1403, without identifying any source food, according to eFoodAlert.

This is the second romaine outbreak in 2026 closed this way: an E. coli O157:H7 outbreak, ref #1382, involving 14 cases and first posted July 1, was also tied to romaine with no grower or brand made public, according to the FDA table and the Marler Blog.

The pattern raises a question the FDA has not answered publicly: when an outbreak's source is named only after the food is gone and no producer is identified, what can consumers — or the stores and restaurants that sold the food — actually do with the information?
